---
title: "Singular fits"
execute: {warning: false, message: false}
---

We represented [group deviations](random-effect-correlations.qmd) with a covariance matrix. Before using that matrix to diagnose a model, let us slow down and recall what its dimensions mean. A two by two covariance matrix tracks variation in two quantities: the first row and column belong to intercept deviations, while the second row and column belong to slope deviations.

The **rank** of a matrix counts how many genuinely distinct directions the matrix can represent. A two by two matrix

$$
\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}
$$

has rank two when neither column is a scalar multiple of the other. By contrast,

$$
\begin{pmatrix}a&ka\\c&kc\end{pmatrix}
$$

has rank one because the second column is $k$ times the first. It may be written with two columns, but the second contributes no new direction. A
[**singular fit**](https://lme4.github.io/lme4/reference/isSingular.html) occurs
when the estimated covariance matrix has lower rank than the formula allows.

The [group deviation model](fixed-and-random-effects.qmd) assigns unobserved group deviations a [covariance matrix](../random-variables-and-distributions/variance-and-covariance.qmd); standard deviations and correlations are alternative summaries of that matrix. Conditional [independence](../foundations/independence.qmd) and the [residual](residuals.qmd) describe the remaining model for individual trials. A rank collapse reports what this repeated MALD design can support under the model. It does not establish that participant or item variation is absent from the population.

We first connect rank to covariance dimensions, then fit a predeclared MALD stress test, inspect the collapsed direction, and separate singularity from optimizer convergence.

## Rank and covariance dimensions

Suppose a grouping term requests $q$ random effect dimensions with covariance matrix $\boldsymbol\Sigma$. A nonsingular fit requires

$$
\operatorname{rank}(\boldsymbol\Sigma)=q.
$$

We now name the geometry. An **eigenvector** of a covariance matrix is a
direction whose orientation stays the same when the matrix acts on it. Its
**eigenvalue** records the variance along that direction, so the contour extends
a distance proportional to the square root of that eigenvalue. The
[two-dimensional PCA
picture](../factorization/principal-component-analysis.qmd#eigenvectors-as-preserved-directions)
shows the corresponding matrix transformation directly.

The fitted MALD example below visualizes this geometry using the standard deviations along the covariance directions estimated from the observed responses. A direction at zero appears as a collapsed bar rather than an arbitrary drawn contour.

The **eigendecomposition** collects the eigenvectors as the columns of
\(\mathbf Q\) and their eigenvalues along the diagonal of
\(\boldsymbol\Lambda\):

$$
\boldsymbol\Sigma
=\mathbf Q\boldsymbol\Lambda\mathbf Q^{\mathsf T}.
$$

Because a covariance matrix cannot have negative variance directions, its rank
is the number of positive eigenvalues in $\boldsymbol\Lambda$. If one
eigenvalue is zero, one linear combination of the requested deviations has no
fitted variation and

$$
\operatorname{rank}(\boldsymbol\Sigma)<q.
$$

In a two-dimensional intercept-slope model, singularity can arise when a
variance reaches zero or when the correlation reaches an endpoint. In a larger
structure, a collapsed dimension may involve a combination of several terms
and may not be obvious from any one printed variance. PCA later uses the same
geometry to find high-variance data directions. Here we use it diagnostically.

## Fitting a predeclared MALD stress test

The stress-test model asks participants to vary in an intercept, frequency slope, duration slope, trial-order slope, and frequency-by-duration interaction slope. It also gives words a trial-order slope. The fixed interaction remains in both models because the diagnostic concerns the group covariance structure.

Before fitting, the design audit asks whether each requested slope's predictor varies within its group. Frequency, duration, trial order, and their frequency-by-duration product vary within participants. Trial order varies within words because the same word occurs at different points for different participants. This support is necessary, but it does not guarantee that the data estimate all variances and correlations away from a boundary.

Both fits use the
[restricted Gaussian objective](fixed-and-random-effects.qmd#gaussian-mixed-model-likelihood).
The restricted log likelihood measures fit after accounting for the common
population coefficient directions, while the numerical gradient checks whether
the optimizer has stopped near a stationary point of that objective.

```{r}
#| label: mald-singular
library(lme4)
library(ggplot2)

mald <- read.csv("data/mald/mald-connected-trials.csv")
mald <- subset(mald, correct == 1L)

standardize <- function(x) {
  as.numeric(scale(x))
}

mald$z_frequency <- standardize(mald$log_frequency_subtlex)
mald$z_duration <- standardize(mald$log_duration)
mald$z_trial <- standardize(mald$trial_order)

fit_control <- lmerControl(
  optimizer = "bobyqa",
  optCtrl = list(maxfun = 200000L)
)

overfit <- lmer(
  log_rt ~ z_frequency * z_duration + z_trial +
    (1 + z_frequency * z_duration + z_trial | participant_id) +
    (1 + z_trial | item),
  data = mald,
  REML = TRUE,
  control = fit_control
)

revised <- lmer(
  log_rt ~ z_frequency * z_duration + z_trial +
    (1 + z_frequency + z_duration + z_trial | participant_id) +
    (1 + z_trial | item),
  data = mald,
  REML = TRUE,
  control = fit_control
)

singularity_check <- c(
  interaction_slope_model = isSingular(overfit, tol = 1e-4),
  revised_model = isSingular(revised, tol = 1e-4)
)
singularity_check

profiled_reml_gradient <- function(model) {
  numDeriv::grad(
    getME(model, "devfun"),
    getME(model, "theta"),
    method = "Richardson"
  )
}

overfit_gradient <- profiled_reml_gradient(overfit)
revised_gradient <- profiled_reml_gradient(revised)
stopifnot(
  length(overfit_gradient) == length(getME(overfit, "theta")),
  length(revised_gradient) == length(getME(revised, "theta")),
  all(is.finite(overfit_gradient)),
  all(is.finite(revised_gradient))
)

objective_check <- data.frame(
  model = c("Interaction slope requested", "Interaction slope removed"),
  restricted_log_likelihood = c(
    as.numeric(logLik(overfit)),
    as.numeric(logLik(revised))
  ),
  maximum_absolute_gradient = c(
    max(abs(overfit_gradient)),
    max(abs(revised_gradient))
  )
)
objective_check
```

`isSingular(..., tol = 1e-4)` declares a fitted covariance direction effectively
zero relative to the fitted scale at that numerical tolerance. This diagnostic
describes the fitted model rather than proving a population claim. A different
tolerance can change a borderline flag, so the rotated standard deviations
below remain part of the evidence.

The model requesting participant interaction-slope variation is singular. Removing only that unsupported random slope gives the prespecified nonsingular revision. This comparison does not remove the fixed frequency-by-duration interaction or the item trial-order slope.

The objective table separates fit from computation. The restricted log
likelihoods describe two different covariance structures with the same
population predictors. The maximum gradient components report whether each
numerical search reached a locally stationary point. Neither quantity tells us
whether the fitted covariance matrix has full rank, which is why the singularity
check remains separate.

## Inspecting the fitted dimensions

`rePCA()` rotates each fitted covariance matrix into orthogonal directions. Here *orthogonal* means perpendicular: movement along one rotated direction does not contain movement along another. The returned standard deviations are the square roots of the rotated, residual scaled eigenvalues. A value near zero marks a direction in which the fitted model has almost no variation.

```{r}
#| label: mald-singular-dimensions
overfit_sd <- rePCA(overfit)$participant_id$sdev
revised_sd <- rePCA(revised)$participant_id$sdev

dimension_table <- rbind(
  data.frame(
    model = "Interaction slope requested",
    dimension = seq_along(overfit_sd),
    orthogonal_sd = overfit_sd
  ),
  data.frame(
    model = "Interaction slope removed",
    dimension = seq_along(revised_sd),
    orthogonal_sd = revised_sd
  )
)
dimension_table
```

The final participant direction in the larger model collapses to the boundary. Because the rotated directions are linear combinations, this fact is stronger than merely inspecting whether one named standard deviation looks small.

```{r}
#| label: singularity-plot
ggplot(
  dimension_table,
  aes(x = factor(dimension), y = orthogonal_sd)
) +
  geom_col(width = 0.72, fill = "grey55") +
  facet_wrap(~model) +
  labs(
    x = "Participant covariance dimension",
    y = "Orthogonal SD (residual-scaled)"
  ) +
  theme_classic()
```

## Separating singularity from convergence

An optimizer can reach a boundary optimum successfully, producing a singular fit without a convergence failure. Conversely, a nonsingular covariance estimate can accompany an optimizer warning. `isSingular()` and the optimizer diagnostics answer different questions and both should be checked.

`bobyqa` is used because the stress test has many bounded covariance parameters; `maxfun = 200000` gives that optimizer more evaluations than its default. <!-- dqr-allow: algorithm-setting --> Neither choice adds information to the design. A boundary estimate concerns the fitted optimum, a convergence warning concerns whether the optimizer reached an adequate optimum, and nonidentifiability concerns whether distinct parameter values imply indistinguishable behavior. These problems may coincide, but they are not synonyms.

A singular fit should send us back to the design: which predictor contrasts vary
within which groups, how many group levels support the covariance, and which
population variation the scientific claim requires. Plausible responses include
removing an unsupported correlation, removing an unsupported slope, collecting
more within-group contrasts, or using a model with **regularization**, a penalty
or prior that discourages weakly supported parameter values; the
[ridge regression](ridge-regression.qmd) develops the penalty version.
These moves encode different population assumptions.

The decision sequence is: (i) inventory contrasts within each group before fitting, (ii) inspect convergence and rank separately, (iii) identify the collapsed covariance direction, (iv) apply the prespecified revision tied to the scientific target, and (v) refit and report the changed population assumption. The MALD revision removes only the collapsed participant interaction slope. It is not a general stepwise selection recipe, and it should not be used to search for a preferred fixed effect conclusion.

## Recap and check

1. Does a singular fit necessarily mean optimizer failure? No. The optimizer may successfully locate a boundary optimum.
2. Does increasing `maxfun` repair an unsupported random slope? No. It gives the optimizer more evaluations while leaving the information in the design unchanged.

We next carry the same group variation logic to a binary linguistic response with [generalized linear mixed models](generalized-linear-mixed-models.qmd).
